analysis.one_liner: Shields hospitals and health workers from lawsuits over care given or withheld during the COVID-19 emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in May 2021 with 3 cosponsors, it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then a subcommittee on November 9, 2021, and died there when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred lawsuits against hospitals, nursing homes, clinics, and health workers for nearly any harm caused by care related to the COVID-19 emergency — including care they chose to withhold and care delivered short-staffed — as long as they acted in good faith. It would have overridden state laws that allowed patients to sue, except in cases of gross negligence, willful misconduct, or intoxication. Patients and families who were harmed would have had almost no legal recourse.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospitals, nursing homes, medical clinics, and the doctors and nurses affiliated with them. They would be immune from lawsuits over COVID-era care — including care refused because of the pandemic and care compromised by pandemic-driven staffing shortages — unless the conduct was grossly negligent, willful or criminal misconduct, reckless, or done under the influence of alcohol or drugs. Their insurers would also gain from fewer claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hospitals, nursing homes, and their malpractice insurers

how_it_helps.text: A covered provider is not liable under any federal or state law for harm caused by an act or omission in providing COVID-related health services in good faith, including services outside the provider's normal area of practice [S2][S3].
The immunity also covers services that were withheld for reasons related to the COVID-19 pandemic, and omissions due to a lack of resources including manpower [S3].
The protection applies during the emergency period plus 60 days after it ends, and preempts state law except where state law already gives providers greater protection from liability [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients and families harmed by substandard pandemic-era care — including neglected nursing home residents and hospital patients short-changed by understaffing — would lose the right to sue for ordinary negligence. Taxpayers and health programs would absorb the costs that families would otherwise recover through the courts.

drawbacks.text: The bill immunizes providers for services they withheld for COVID-related reasons and for omissions caused by a lack of manpower, which could shield nursing homes and hospitals from lawsuits over understaffed, neglectful care during the deadliest stretch of the pandemic [S3].

It would preempt state tort law — the state-level rules that let injured patients hold providers accountable — leaving harmed families without recourse unless they could prove the extreme exceptions like gross negligence [S3].

The good-faith case for it: emergency conditions and shifting federal guidance made normal medical standards hard to meet, and some workers practiced outside their usual specialty to help; shielding them was framed as keeping volunteers in the fight. The bill does keep gross negligence, willful misconduct, and intoxication outside the shield [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection for individual clinicians who volunteered beyond their training is the most defensible part. But the bill goes far beyond that, handing hospitals and nursing homes immunity for care withheld or delivered short-staffed and overriding the state laws patients rely on. The cost falls entirely on people who were already the pandemic's victims. On balance, the shield serves institutions more than patients.

outcome.mechanism: It never got a vote: the House Judiciary Committee sent it to a subcommittee in November 2021, no hearing or markup ever followed, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Lou Correa introduced the bill on May 7, 2021, with Rep. Michael Burgess as an original cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1][S3][S5].
The bill had 3 cosponsors in total, 2 Republicans and 1 Democrat [S4].
On November 9, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties, and no further action was taken before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients and families came out ahead in the narrow sense that they kept the full right to sue over substandard COVID-era care; hospitals and nursing homes never received the immunity they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients kept their right to sue

industries.note: The bill would give them sweeping immunity for COVID-era care, including care withheld and care compromised by staffing shortages, while patients harmed by that care lose their day in court.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care facilities
industries.note: Explicitly covered as 'related health care entities,' nursing homes — the setting with the highest COVID death tolls — would be shielded from lawsuits over neglect and understaffing during the emergency.
A near-total bar on negligence claims for COVID-era care means far fewer claims and payouts; the saving comes directly out of compensation that injured patients and families would otherwise receive.

industries.industry: Physicians, nurses, and other licensed health professionals
industries.note: Individual clinicians get immunity for good-faith care, including work outside their normal specialty — protection that arguably kept emergency volunteers in place — but the same shield also covers negligent institutional care they work within.
